dek: Trace privacy controls, connected AI telemetry and a safeguard against lost spans.

stories.title: LangSmith restricts sensitive trace content by group and metadata
stories.summary: Enterprise administrators can limit who sees trace inputs and outputs while allowing access to operational details, and set policies using groups and root-run metadata.
body: LangSmith is an agent engineering platform that records traces so developers can debug agent behavior. Those traces can contain customer messages and model responses alongside the run tree and timing information engineers need. LangChain says teams have had to choose between maintaining duplicate traces and workspaces or giving up visibility into production activity.

The new controls separate access to inputs and outputs from access to other trace data. First, administrators can allow engineers to inspect run trees, latency and token usage while restricting sensitive content. Next, they can organize users into groups and define permissions for each workspace, layered with existing role and attribute controls. Finally, trace-level policies can check metadata on the root run, such as a customer or user identifier, to determine which traces a person may access.

The company says the controls can be combined: for example, support staff could see content for their own customers while engineers inspect performance across traces without seeing inputs or outputs. Full traces remain stored in LangSmith, so these are access controls rather than redaction. The features are available on Enterprise plans.
stories.takeaway: Teams using production traces with sensitive content can review their access policies and root metadata before widening debugging access.

stories.title: Logz.io connects AI request timelines with infrastructure telemetry
stories.summary: A new AI observability capability connects model, retrieval and tool steps to the logs, traces and infrastructure behind a run.
body: Logz.io is an observability platform for examining logs, metrics and traces. It has announced an AI observability capability for teams operating agents and language model applications. The company says a slow or incorrect agent response can originate in a retrieval store, downstream service or infrastructure, leaving engineers to assemble the explanation across separate systems.

The proposed workflow starts with an AI request shown as a searchable, filterable trace. An engineer can open the run as a timeline and inspect the inputs and outputs of model, retrieval and tool steps, alongside the associated logs, backend traces and infrastructure. The announcement also describes a comparison of groups of runs to surface attributes shared by failures, token counts for steps and runs, and alerts through an account's existing alerting setup.

Logz.io says the capability ingests OpenTelemetry Protocol and OpenLLMetry data, allowing teams already using the latter to send their existing instrumentation without adopting a proprietary software development kit. The announcement describes product capabilities and the company's own use, but supplies no independent performance measurements. Customers can request access.
stories.takeaway: Teams already sending compatible telemetry can assess whether linking agent steps to infrastructure helps their investigations, subject to access availability.

stories.title: Phoenix rejects a tracing configuration that could silently drop spans
stories.summary: Phoenix tracing helpers now reject a positional exporter argument and warn when certain environment settings are ignored.
body: Arize Phoenix is an open-source platform for observing and evaluating AI applications. Its tracing package helps configure OpenTelemetry, which records operations as spans. The release notes describe a configuration mistake that could drop every span silently when an exporter was passed positionally to a span processor instead of inside an options object.

The updated batch and simple processors now throw a type error for that positional form, making the mistake visible. The registration helper also accepts a sampler, which controls which traces are recorded, and span limits, and re-exports several sampler implementations. It warns once per applicable environment variable when settings for sampling, spans, attributes or batch processing are set but the corresponding option is not configured in code, because the underlying OpenTelemetry JavaScript release ignores those variables. For batch settings with custom processors, the warning comes from the re-exported batch processor. The release notes do not report how many deployments encountered the issue.
stories.takeaway: JavaScript teams upgrading Phoenix tracing should check processor construction and heed warnings about ignored telemetry settings.

image_provenance.prompt: Create a landscape newspaper infographic based on https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix/releases/tag/%40arizeai/phoenix-otel%403.1.0. Explain one change: a tracing span processor now rejects an incorrectly supplied exporter argument with an error rather than silently dropping spans. Conceptual comparison, no claim about measured results. Warm newsprint, dark ink, restrained red and teal, large readable type, simple arrows. Exact labels: 'Exporter argument', 'Old: spans dropped', 'Now: configuration error'. No other technical claims, numbers, logos, footer or watermark.

stories.score_reason: Explicitly catches a configuration error that could otherwise silently lose all spans.
